page: Google Cloud Platform c4n-highmem-48 is a network-oriented, memory-expanded virtual machine configuration designed for data-intensive processing and memory-heavy workloads. Driven by an x86_64 Intel Xeon 8581C processor clocked at 2.3 GHz, the instance provides 48 dedicated vCPUs distributed across 24 physical cores with multithreading enabled. The CPU subsystem features a 260 MB shared L3 cache alongside support for advanced instruction sets including AVX-512 and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX). Memory capacity totals 372 GB, providing approximately 7.75 GB of RAM per vCPU without any bundled local storage or discrete GPU accelerators.

Benchmark results show competitive computational and cryptographic throughput. The server registered a Geekbench single-core score of 2,247, placing it in the top decile, alongside strong Geekbench multi-core performance of 19,286. Execution of vector and specialized workloads is bolstered by AMX and AVX-512 extensions, yielding strong results across image processing, text processing, and PassMark extended instruction evaluations. Decompression benchmarks also demonstrated robust scale, reaching 328.47 GB/sec in multi-threaded bzip3 decompression.

Data handling benchmarks reflect solid performance profiles. Cached memory operations reached 3,887.58 GB/sec, while uncached large-block reads and writes attained 144.42 GB/sec and 61.75 GB/sec, respectively. In-memory data store testing showed 56.07 million operations per second on Redis SET benchmarks, while web serving throughput achieved 73.86 GB/sec. CPU-driven inference tests revealed high responsiveness on smaller language models, delivering 388.63 tokens per second on 135M model generation and 244.54 tokens per second on 7B model prompt processing.

Because the c4n-highmem-48 lacks attached local NVMe drives and GPU hardware, all persistence depends entirely on remote network storage, and heavy matrix acceleration relies strictly on host CPU instructions. Consequently, this configuration fits large in-memory caching layers, medium-scale relational databases, data transformation pipelines, static web traffic handling, and lightweight CPU-bound inference services requiring substantial memory footprints.
